content: The relevant impurity must be clearly identified by name. Analytical methods used to assess the impurity must be peer-validated. For determining the minimum effective period of a refill bottle for a liquid vaporizer, no suitable test methods are currently available. Unless otherwise specified, storage conditions should follow the guidelines outlined in Section 2 of this manual. Samples of the formulation, taken both before and after storage stability testing, should be analyzed concurrently after the test to minimize analytical errors. Regarding aerosol dispensers, not all characteristics defining their acceptability are included in the provided specification guidelines. The flammability and ignition distance of the spray produced by the dispenser and its formulation are critical for user safety and must be addressed through appropriate labeling. Aerosol dispensers are expected to resist corrosion for at least two years from the date of release by the manufacturer. Ideally, specifications would include a clause defining the corrosion resistance of the dispenser, but no practical method currently exists to predict whether the structural integrity of the dispenser will remain uncompromised within two years. Manufacturers, users, and other stakeholders are encouraged to develop and propose simple methods under standard conditions to address this gap. When preparing draft specifications, clauses should not be omitted or additional clauses inserted, nor should limits be made more lenient than those provided in the guidelines, without referencing Section 4. If two or more active ingredients are co-formulated, they should have separate specifications. Aerosol dispensers must comply with the specifications when sampled from any part of the consignment using the procedure described in Note 1 or another acceptable method. The product should consist of a liquid formulation in a pressurized, non-refillable aerosol dispenser containing propellants, synergists, and other formulants as required, intended for releasing the active ingredient into the air as an aerosol. The active ingredient must pass an identity test and, if its identity remains uncertain, must comply with at least one additional test. The minimum net content of the formulation must be declared, and the average net content, when determined, must not be less than the declared value. Aerosol dispenser valves must not clog when tested according to the procedure described in Note 11 or another acceptable method. The combined weight of the container and its contents must not fall below a specified percentage of the original weight. Sampling requirements include storing samples to prevent material deterioration, using clean and dry sampling instruments, and protecting samples from contamination. Any sample failing to meet the requirements is considered defective. The acceptance number is the maximum number of defective samples permissible for a lot to be accepted. The discharge rate of an aerosol dispenser is determined by measuring the quantity of material expelled through the valve over a specified time, typically 10 seconds. The temperature of the dispenser must be carefully controlled for reproducibility. The test is usually repeated three times for accuracy, but for products with vapor-phase tap valves, the discharge interval may be reduced to 5 seconds, and the number of determinations to two, to minimize composition variation during spraying. Long-lasting insecticidal nets (LNs) are made of monoor multi-filament fibers with one or more active ingredients incorporated into or coated onto the filaments. Combination LNs may consist of different netting materials treated with different active ingredients. Specifications for combination LNs should be split into one for each netting material and one for the finished net. Systematic variations in active ingredient content across or along netting could compromise efficacy, quality control, and safety. If systematic variation is suspected, special sampling procedures should be designed to test for its presence. Acceptable performance of LNs is defined by WHO as retention of biological activity through 20 standard washes. WHO specifications should provide limits and methods to indicate whether retention or release of active ingredients occurs but cannot guarantee acceptable efficacy before or after 20 standard washes. For coated LNs, if the netting is manufactured under different deniers, the active ingredient content must be specified for each type of denier. If the active ingredient content is also specified as mg/m² of netting, it should be calculated from values for active ingredient in g/kg and mass of net/m².
